raw_response:
Fifty years I been working this same ground. My father farmed here, I farmed here, and I do what I always do. I don't change much. Changing is risky—you never know if the new thing works, but you know if the old thing fails.

My 12 mu I split like this: 7 mu is my wheat-maize ground. Winter I plant wheat, summer after I cut it I put maize on the same soil. Then I got 5 mu separate for cotton. That cotton ground has been cotton ground for thirty years. Cotton is hard work, but the money is okay.

For the **wheat**, I go to the village supply shop in October before planting. I buy 7 bags of compound fertilizer—the 100-jin bags, that 15-15-15 kind—one bag per mu. I spread it all before I seed. Then in March when the wheat is growing tall and hungry, I throw about 15 jin of urea per mu on top. That is what my neighbor Old Zhang does, and his wheat is as good as mine. I water 3 times: before the ground freezes, in spring when it is shooting up, and when the grain is filling out. I spray twice for aphids and rust. After the maize in autumn, I run the rotary tiller to break up the stalks and loosen the soil before I seed wheat.

For **maize**, right after wheat harvest in June, I go straight into the ground—no tilling, just seed into the stubble. Everyone here does this now. Hybrid seed from the village shop. I put down some compound when I seed, then around when the stalks reach my shoulder, I come back with 20 jin of urea per mu. I water once or twice depending on how the rain comes. Maize doesn't need as much work. Two sprays for the stem borer.

**Cotton** is the hardest and the most worrying. In spring I plow the cotton ground deep—proper plow, not just rotary. I plant improved seed, the kind the town shop sells. I fertilize several times through the season. I worry most about bollworm. If I skip a spray or spray late, the worm gets into the bolls and half the harvest is gone. I saw this happen to my cousin two years back. He lost almost everything. So I spray 5 times on the cotton, sometimes more if I see the moths coming. I water 4 times with the pump.

I don't change my quantities much year to year. A little extra fertilizer means I don't lose sleep about yield. A bad harvest is a real disaster. Wasting some fertilizer is just money—bad, but survivable.
